parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

**GNP Sportswear **

GNP Sportswear is a medium-sized clothing manufacturer based in Country X that specialises in producing high-quality sportswear and athletic shoes. GNP has been in business for 15 years and employs 250 people. Its main factory uses batch production methods to manufacture products. GNP sources raw materials locally and imports some specialised fabrics from neighbouring countries.

GNP Sportswear sells its products primarily through sports retailers in Country X. The company has a small but growing online presence, with 10% of its sales now coming from its e-commerce website. GNP is considering expanding its online sales channel to reach more customers directly.

The company's annual revenue last year was \$30 million, with a net profit of \$2.4 million. However, rising costs of raw materials and increased competition from cheaper imported brands have put pressure on GNP's profit margins. The management team is exploring ways to reduce costs and increase efficiency.

GNP Sportswear is also facing challenges related to changing consumer preferences. There is a growing demand for environmentally friendly and sustainable products in the sportswear market. The company is considering investing in new production methods and materials to create a line of eco-friendly sportswear.

Country X is a developing economy. The government of Country X has recently announced plans to reduce import tariffs on textiles and finished garments. This change could lead to increased competition from foreign brands but also potentially lower costs for some of GNP's imported materials.

GNP's Human Resources department has noticed an increase in employee turnover in the past year. The company is looking at ways to improve employee retention and motivation.

**Appendix 1: Extract from GNP Sportswear's website **

| At GNP Sportswear, we're passionate about creating high-quality sportswear that helps you perform at your best. Our products are designed for comfort, durability, and style. Shop our range of athletic wear and shoes for all your sporting needs. Free shipping on orders over \$100! |
| --- |

**Appendix 2: GNP Sportswear's Annual Sales Data **

| Year 1 | \$25 million |
| :---: | :---: |
| Year 2 | \$27 million |
| Year 3 | \$30 million |
| Year 4 | \$32 million (forecast) |

Consider how the following three methods might help GNP Sportswear improve employee retention and motivation:

- Introduce a performance-related bonus scheme
- Implement a staff training and development programme
- Offer flexible working hours

Which method is likely to be most effective? Justify your choice.

Refer to the following [insert](https://cdn.savemyexams.com/uploads/2024/10/gnp-sportswear-case-study.pdf) when answering the question.
parts.solution_md:
Introducing a performance-related bonus scheme could motivate employees to work harder and be more productive. This financial reward might encourage staff to stay with the company longer **[An] **to earn bonuses, which would reverse the increase in staff turnover **[An]**. However, it could create unhealthy competition between workers or cause stress if targets are too high **[An]**

Implementing a staff training programme would help employees gain new skills and feel more valued. This could increase job satisfaction and make workers want to stay at GNP **[An]**. Training could also improve efficiency and product quality. But it would be expensive and time-consuming to run courses. Given that GNP's profit margins are under pressure **[Ap]**, this option may not be acceptable **[An]**

Offering flexible working hours would give employees a better work-life balance. This could reduce stress and make staff happier in their jobs, encouraging them to stay **[An]**. It may also help GNP attract new employees. However, it could be difficult to manage production schedules for GNP's sportswear range **[Ap] **with varied working hours **[An]**

Overall, the staff training programme is likely to be most effective **[E]**. GNP has experienced increased employee turnover **[Ap]**, so developing workers' skills would make them feel more valued and less likely to leave. Training would also help GNP adapt to changing consumer preferences for eco-friendly products **[Ap]**. While expensive initially, the long-term benefits of increased productivity and retention would outweigh the costs **[E]**. The other options may help, but they don't address the core issue **[E] **of making employees feel invested in the company's ambitions for the future **[Ap]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Structure**
> 
> - Write one PEA paragraph for each point identified in the question:
> 
>   - Point: Identify the problem
>   - Evidence (Ap): Apply case study detail
>   - Analysis (An): Explain business impact
> - Add a final Evaluation (E):
> 
>   - Decide which problem is easiest/hardest to overcome
>   - Justify your choice
>   - Compare and reject alternatives
> 
> **Marking approach**
> 
> - This is a levelled response answer in which the examiner determines how well you have demonstrated skills of application, analysis and evaluation
> 
>   - Application (4) – Use case study facts
>   - Analysis (4) – Chain effects clearly, using business terms
>   - Evaluation (4) – Balanced judgement, rejects others with reasoning
> 
> **Mark scheme**
> 
> - **Performance-related bonus scheme**
> 
>   - **Advantages**
>   
>     - Links pay to individual or team performance → staff see direct reward for meeting targets → boosts motivation and productivity
>     - Can reinforce company goals (e.g. quality, efficiency) → aligns employee effort with GNP’s objectives
>   - **Disadvantages**
>   
>     - Adds variable labour cost → reduces net margin on \$2.4 m profit
>     - May demotivate staff if targets are perceived as unattainable or unfair
>     - Administrative complexity in measuring and distributing bonuses → HR burden
> - **Staff training and development programme**
> 
>   - **Advantages**
>   
>     - Up-skills 250 production and batch-line workers → increases job competence and confidence
>     - Demonstrates investment in employee career growth → improves retention and loyalty
>     - Helps GNP adapt to eco-friendly production methods → supports strategic shift toward sustainable sportswear
>   - **Disadvantages**
>   
>     - Training time off the line → temporary dip in output and potential backlog
>     - Requires upfront investment in trainers and materials → short-term cost without immediate sales impact
> - **Flexible working hours**
> 
>   - **Advantages**
>   
>     - Better work–life balance → reduces absenteeism and turnover in a developing-economy labour market
>     - Can attract diverse talent (e.g. parents, students) → widens recruitment pool
>   - **Disadvantages**
>   
>     - Factory batch-production schedules may limit flexibility → operational complexity
>     - Difficult to coordinate shifts → risk of understaffing or overtime pay
> - **Conclusion**
> 
>   - Training and development is the most effective method for GNP because it directly addresses skill gaps, supports the company’s sustainability goals and shows long-term commitment to employees, driving retention in a competitive market
>   - Performance bonuses can boost productivity but add variable costs and risk uneven motivation
>   - Flexible hours improve work–life balance but are hard to implement in batch-production factories and may disrupt scheduling

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

DEF Fashions (DEF)

DEF is a medium-sized clothing and fashion accessories manufacturer based in Country X. Established 25 years ago as a private limited company, it has grown steadily and now employs 250 people across its two factories and head office. DEF specialises in producing trendy, affordable clothing and accessories for budget high-street retailers.

The fast fashion industry has become increasingly competitive, with pressure to reduce costs and improve speed to market. DEF's sales have remained stable over the past two years, but profits have declined (see Appendix 1). The CEO is considering investing in automation technology to increase production efficiency and reduce labour costs. Staff have expressed significant concerns about this, and there have been discussions with trade unions regarding possible industrial action. 

DEF currently manufactures all its products in Country X. It struggles to recruit and retain staff, and productivity is low. It is investigating the possibility of outsourcing some production to countries with lower labour costs to improve profit margins. 

The government of Country X has recently introduced new regulations requiring clothing manufacturers to disclose their supply chain and ensure fair labour practices. DEF is evaluating the potential impact on its operations and relationships with suppliers.

Appendix 1: DEF Financial Data

| Year | Revenue (\$m) | Profit (\$m) | Unit produced (millions) |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| 2021 | 78.5 | 5.2 | 15.7 |
| 2022 | 79.1 | 4.8 | 15.2 |
| 2023 | 79.8 | 4.5 | 15.1 |

Consider the advantages and disadvantages of the following two options for DEF to improve the motivation of staff in its factories:

- Implement a profit-sharing scheme
- Implement job rotation for production workers

Which option should DEF choose? Justify your answer.

Refer to the following [insert](https://cdn.savemyexams.com/uploads/2024/10/def-fashions-def.pdf) when answering the question.
parts.solution_md:
A profit-sharing scheme could motivate factory workers by giving them a financial stake in the company's success **[An]**. According to Herzberg, financial rewards can reduce dissatisfaction. It may encourage higher productivity and efficiency, which DEF needs to improve its declining profits** [Ap]**. However, profit-sharing can be expensive to implement and may not address underlying issues causing low motivation **[An]**, most notably the business's plans for automation **[Ap]**

Job rotation can reduce boredom and increase job satisfaction by adding variety, which Herzberg suggests may be a key motivator **[An]**. It may improve workers' skills and understanding of the whole production process, giving the business much-needed flexibility **[An]** as many staff leave **[Ap]**. However, it could temporarily reduce efficiency as workers learn new roles, and some employees may resist change **[An]**

Overall, DEF should implement job rotation for production workers **[E]**. This directly addresses the issue of low productivity in the factories **[Ap]**. It is likely to be less costly than profit-sharing, which is important given DEF's falling profits **[Ap]**. Job rotation also aligns with the need to improve efficiency **[E]** and could help DEF adapt to new regulations on fair labour practices **[Ap]**. While profit-sharing has merits, job rotation is a more targeted solution to DEF's specific challenges in motivating factory workers **[E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Structure**
> 
> - Write one PEA paragraph for each point identified in the question:
> 
>   - Point: Identify the problem
>   - Evidence (Ap): Apply case study detail
>   - Analysis (An): Explain business impact
> - Add a final Evaluation (E):
> 
>   - Decide which problem is easiest/hardest to overcome
>   - Justify your choice
>   - Compare and reject alternatives
> 
> **Marking approach**
> 
> - This is a levelled response answer in which the examiner determines how well you have demonstrated skills of application, analysis and evaluation
> 
>   - Application (4) – Use case study facts
>   - Analysis (4) – Chain effects clearly, using business terms
>   - Evaluation (4) – Balanced judgement, rejects others with reasoning
> 
> **Mark scheme**
> 
> - **Profit-sharing scheme**
> 
>   - **Advantages**
>   
>     - Links pay directly to company profit → staff see direct reward for improved performance → boosts motivation and productivity
>     - Can reduce risk of industrial action by giving employees a stake in outcomes
>     - Encourages teamwork as everyone benefits from collective success
>   - **Disadvantages**
>   
>     - DEF’s profits have fallen from \$5.2 m in 2021 to \$4.5 m in 2023 → limited surplus to share → scheme may be seen as tokenistic
>     - Requires complex administration and clear rules on eligibility → adds HR cost
>     - Rewards high performers and low performers equally → may demotivate top talent
> - **Job rotation for production workers**
> 
>   - **Advantages**
>   
>     - Reduces boredom and repetitive strain → increases job satisfaction and lowers turnover in factories struggling to retain staff
>     - Broadens employee skills → more flexible workforce that can cover absences without overtime
>     - Low implementation cost (uses existing staff and roles)
>   - **Disadvantages**
>   
>     - Initial training time reduces output temporarily → may worsen low productivity in the short run
>     - Workers may feel insecure if moved into unfamiliar tasks → potential mistakes or quality issues
>     - Requires careful planning to avoid production bottlenecks
> - **Recommendation**
> 
>   - DEF should implement job rotation first
>   
>     - It addresses low morale and high turnover immediately with minimal cash outlay
>     - Builds a multiskilled workforce and reduces the risk of industrial disputes without relying on limited profits
>   - Once productivity and retention improve, DEF can revisit a scaled-back profit-sharing scheme to reinforce long-term commitment

parts.problem_md: Do you think job enrichment is a better way for a business to motivate its employees than profit sharing? Justify your answer.
parts.solution_md:
Job enrichment allows businesses to fully utilise employees' skills, increasing labour flexibility **[K]**. This can lead to higher productivity as workers feel more valued from greater job satisfaction and being challenged at work. However, some workers may not want more complex work, which could lead to mistakes or waste **[An]**

Profit sharing can motivate employees with money, which many find important **[K]**. It builds team spirit and creates a common goal to increase the business's financial performance. However,  if the business makes little or no profit, there's nothing to share, which could decrease motivation rather than increase it **[An]**

Overall, job enrichment is better **[E]** because it makes jobs more interesting daily, while profit sharing only happens periodically, usually once a year. Job enrichment is more likely to motivate employees regularly, having a bigger impact on their effort and productivity throughout the year **[E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - You are writing a mini-argument with a decision
> 
>   - Give one relevant reason to support your view → 1 K mark
>   - Explain why this reason helps the business (cause-effect chain) →  1 An mark
>   - Give a different possible reason or viewpoint → 1 K mark
>   - Explain why this could also help the business → 1 An mark
>   - Make a decision — which argument is stronger or more important overall? → up to 2 E marks
> 
> **Mark scheme**
> 
> - Points might include
> 
>   - Job enrichment:
>   
>     - Business able to make most / full use of employee’s skills [k] which can help increase labour flexibility [an]
>     - Training may be needed [k] which can increase expenses [an]
>     - Workers gain more job satisfaction/ feel recognised/valued [k]
>     - Not all workers are able / want to do more complex work [k] leading to mistakes/ waste [an]
>     - Not easy to add extra tasks to some jobs [k]
>     - Time consuming to redesign tasks [k]
>     - May create conflict between employees (as may not be possible to offer opportunities to all) [k]
>   - Profit sharing:
>   
>     - Money is a major motivator for many employees [k]
>     - Can help build team spirit / sense of belonging / common goal [k]
>     - Not everyone is motivated by money [k]
>     - If business makes low/ no profit, then there is little/ nothing to share [k] which could decrease motivation [an]
>   - Justification might include:
>   
>     - Job enrichment can help the business make the most use of employee’s skills [k] increasing productivity [an]
>     - A business making no profit, has nothing to share [k] which could decrease rather than increase motivation [an]
>     - I think job enrichment is better as making the job more interesting is more likely to motivate employees every day. [eval]. Profit-sharing is at the end of the year, and therefore is likely to have less impact on daily effort.[eval]
>   - Other appropriate responses should also be credited

{align=center} **Soapy Sudds Manufacturer (SSM) **

SSM is a public limited company that was set up 25 years ago. SSM manufacture soap powder in country Y. The soap powder is used for washing clothes. The directors of SSM are considering ways to increase sales. 

SSM has a total of 100 employees with 60 in the Operations Department. It uses flow production in the factory and has 10 production lines with 5 workers and 1 supervisor for each line. The Operations Manager is aware that production workers are unhappy and often complain about their jobs being boring. These workers have always been paid by an hourly rate. The Marketing Director thinks SSM should start selling soap powder in markets in other countries. SSM will need to carry out either primary market research or secondary market research to forecast the potential total sales in these new markets. There are many existing manufacturers in these countries. SSM need to consider the problems when entering new markets in other countries such as tariffs or quotas.

 All the different types of soap powder are manufactured on production lines using flow production. SSM makes use of specialisation.

> Answers such as ‘psychological’ or ‘basic needs’ are not awarded marks as they are too vague

>

> **Mark scheme**
> 
> - Award 1 mark per level (max 2). Two from:

parts.problem_md:
Outline **two **ways MBH can use ideas from Herzberg’s theory to motivate its employees.

> **[case-study]**
> MBH is a business organisation in the public sector. It controls 5 hospitals and has 5600 employees including 440 doctors. External recruitment is used when recruiting skilled employees. The Human Resources Director uses ideas from Herzberg’s theory to improve employee motivation. He is worried about communication barriers within MBH. The business has a tall organisational structure and a long chain of command. Most of MBH’s internal communication is by email and phone calls.
parts.solution_md:
MBH could give hospital employees** [Ap] **more interesting tasks with responsibility **[K]**, one of Herzberg's motivators** **

They could also provide opportunities for promotion** [K]**, which should be possible given MBH's tall organisational structure** [Ap]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Your answer must focus on Herzberg's motivators
> 
> Hygiene factors will not be awarded marks as they prevent demotivation

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - Knowledge 2; Application 2
> 
>   - Give two valid benefits to achieve both knowledge [K] marks
>   - For each benefit, refer to the business case study to achieve both application [Ap] marks
> 
> **Mark scheme**
> 
> - Points might include:
> 
>   - Could give employees more responsibility [k] in the hospital [ap]
>   - Offer more interesting work [k] as many are skilled employees [ap]
>   - Offer more praise for good work [k]
>   - Give chances for promotion [k] as there is a tall organisational structure [ap]
> - Other appropriate responses should also be credited
> - To use words from the stem as application, the reference must be appropriate (i.e. make sense) in relation to the point being made
> 
>   - The following words are likely to be appropriate for this question:
>   
>     - 440 / doctors
>     - Hospitals / or related words
>     - 5600 employees
>     - Public sector
>     - Communication barriers
>     - Phone/email
>     - Long chain of command
>     - Tall organisational structure
>     - Skilled employees
> - Other appropriate examples in context can still be credited
> - Do not award examples of hygiene factors on their own e.g., Pay, improve working conditions as these are not motivators

parts.problem_md: Identify **two **reasons (other than financial) why people work.
parts.solution_md:
People work to achieve job satisfaction as a result of doing a good job **[K]**

parts.problem_md:
Identify the level of Maslow’s Hierarchy of Needs each of the following methods belongs to:

- ‘Employee of the month award’
- Organises team building courses

> **[case-study]**
> GCF is a public limited company. It provides a range of computer services to businesses including designing websites and creating apps. The Human Resources Director use ideas based on Maslow’s Hierarchy of Needs to help keep GCF’s 250 employees well-motivated. An extract of methods used is shown in below. GCF plans to expand by taking over one of its competitors. This will cost \$50m. To finance the takeover, GCF is considering issuing new shares.
> 
> | **Extract of methods used at GCF to motivate employees** |
> |---|
> | ‘Employee of the month’ award |
> | Organises team building courses |
parts.solution_md:
‘Employee of the month award’: Esteem needs **[K]**

Organises team building courses: Social needs **[K]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Self-esteem cannot be accepted as a level in Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs, as the correct term is esteem needs

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - Knowledge 2
> 
>   - Clearly identify two features to achieve both knowledge [K] marks
>   - 1 mark for each valid feature
> 
> **Mark scheme**
> 
> - ‘Employee of the month award’: Level 4 OR esteem
> - Organises team building courses: Level 3 OR social/belonging
> - Do not award self-esteem as an alternative to esteem (as this is not a level)

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

- Award 2 marks for any full definition listed under "Mark scheme" (e.g. "switching between jobs over a period of time", "doing each task for only a limited time") even if "variety" is not stated
- Accept regular or periodic swapping of jobs (e.g. "each year they swap their jobs") as switching between jobs over a period of time
- Award 1 mark only for a partial definition such as "workers do a variety of tasks" or "swapping jobs" with no sense of rotation over time

Define ‘job rotation’.
parts.solution_md:
Job rotation is the process of switching an employee between jobs **[K]**, increasing variety in their jobs **[K]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - Knowledge 2
> 
>   - Give a clearly-stated, valid definition to achieve both knowledge [K] marks
>   - 2 marks for a full definition, 1 mark for a partial definition
> 
> **Mark scheme**
> 
> - Employees swapping around and doing each specific task for only a limited time [2]
> 
>   - OR Process of switching an employee between jobs over a period of time [2]
>   - OR Increasing variety in the workplace by allowing workers to switch from one task to another [2]
> - Partial definition e.g. workers do a variety of tasks [1]

> **[exam-tip]**
> Do not confuse job rotation, which is switching between tasks with the same level of challenge, with job enlargement, which is switching between tasks of varying levels of challenge.
> 
> A definition says what something is, so do not use a benefit such as motivation or less boredom in place of a second defining point.
